concepts.name: Diwan-i-Wizarat: Role and Evolution of the Wazir
key_dimensions: Distinction between a powerful Wazir (e.g., under Firuz Shah Tughluq) vs. a subordinate Wazir (e.g., under Alauddin Khalji) — UPSC trap on whether Wazir was always the most powerful noble
Dual functions: revenue administration (financial) vs. general executive supervision
Comparison with the Mughal Wazir/Diwan to avoid period conflation
How Alauddin Khalji deliberately curtailed Wazir's power and why

concepts.name: Diwan-i-Ariz: Military Department and its Limitations
key_dimensions: Ariz-i-Mamalik was NOT the Commander-in-Chief — a classic UPSC trap; Sultan retained supreme command
Functions: recruitment, payment, equipment inspection (chehra and dagh system)
Alauddin Khalji's use of this department to enforce the branding (dagh) and descriptive roll (chehra) reforms
Distinction from Diwan-i-Wizarat in terms of jurisdiction and overlap in military finance

concepts.name: Dagh and Chehra System under Alauddin Khalji
key_dimensions: Dagh (branding of horses) and Chehra (descriptive roll of soldiers) as anti-corruption military reforms
Purpose: prevent fraud by nobles presenting borrowed horses/soldiers during inspection
Whether this system was continued by subsequent sultans (Firuz Shah Tughluq largely abandoned it — key contrast)
Link to Alauddin's market reforms and broader centralization policy

concepts.name: Diwan-i-Insha: Royal Correspondence and Bureaucratic Sovereignty
key_dimensions: Functions: drafting royal farmans, receiving petitions, maintaining state correspondence
Dabir-i-Khas vs. general Insha scribes — hierarchy within the department
Role in projecting Sultan's sovereignty and legitimacy (all decrees passed through this office)
Comparison with Mughal Maktubat/Mir Munshi system to avoid conflation

concepts.name: Diwan-i-Rasalat: Foreign Affairs and Religious Matters
key_dimensions: Dual role: handling foreign embassies AND supervising religious endowments (waqf) — often confused as two separate departments
UPSC trap: sometimes described purely as a 'foreign affairs' ministry, ignoring its religious jurisdiction
Role of Sadr-us-Sudur as the head dealing with ecclesiastical matters — overlap with Diwan-i-Rasalat
Significance during Tughlaq period when religious policy became more prominent

concepts.name: Sadr-us-Sudur and Qazi-ul-Quzat: Separation of Religious and Judicial Authority
key_dimensions: Sadr-us-Sudur: supervised religious endowments, appointments of religious scholars, enforcement of Shariat
Qazi-ul-Quzat: Chief Justice heading the judicial hierarchy under Islamic law
UPSC trap: whether the same person could hold both offices simultaneously (sometimes they did — e.g., under certain sultans)
Distinction between Qazi (judicial), Muhtasib (censor of public morals), and Sadr (religious grants) — three different offices often confused

concepts.name: Muhtasib: Censor of Public Morality and Market Oversight
key_dimensions: Primary role: enforcing Islamic moral code — prohibition of wine, gambling, unlawful sexual conduct
Secondary role under Alauddin Khalji: extended to market price enforcement (overlap with Shahna-i-Mandi)
UPSC trap: Muhtasib is NOT the same as the market controller (Shahna) — different officers with overlapping jurisdictions under Alauddin
Decline of the office's effectiveness in later Sultanate period

concepts.name: Alauddin Khalji's Market Control System: Four Markets and Their Regulatory Officers
key_dimensions: Four markets: grain market (Shahna-i-Mandi), cloth market, cattle/horse market, general commodities market — UPSC frequently tests the number and types
Three-tier intelligence: Shahna (controller), Barid (secret reporter), Munhiyan (spies) — all reporting independently to Sultan
Price fixation linked to maintaining a large cheap army — economic rationale, not just administrative reform
Why the system collapsed after Alauddin's death: structural dependency on personal autocracy

concepts.name: Iqta System: Evolution from Early to Later Sultanate
key_dimensions: Early Iqta (Iltutmish period): transferable, non-hereditary revenue assignments to Turkish nobles in lieu of salary
Later degeneration: Iqtas becoming quasi-hereditary under weak sultans — UPSC trap on whether Iqtas were always non-hereditary
Firuz Shah Tughluq's formalization of hereditary Iqtas as a deliberate policy — key reversal
Distinction between Iqta (revenue assignment) and Jagir (Mughal period) — avoid anachronistic conflation

concepts.name: Wali/Muqti: Provincial Governor in the Iqta Framework
key_dimensions: Muqti/Wali as the holder of a large Iqta (province) — dual role as revenue collector and military commander
Obligation to maintain a stipulated military contingent from Iqta revenues
Accountability mechanism: Diwan-i-Wizarat's oversight of Muqtis' accounts — how this worked and where it failed
UPSC trap: Muqti is the provincial-level Iqta holder; Amil is the revenue official under him — hierarchy confusion

concepts.name: Revenue Administration: Kharaj, Ushr, Jizya, and Zakat
key_dimensions: Kharaj: land tax on non-Muslim cultivators (typically 1/3 to 1/2 of produce under various sultans — exact fractions tested)
Ushr: tithe (1/10) on Muslim-owned irrigated land vs. 1/20 on rain-fed land — distinction frequently tested
Jizya: poll tax on non-Muslims — UPSC trap: Firuz Shah Tughluq imposed it even on Brahmins who were previously exempt
Distinction between Jizya (per-person) and Kharaj (per-land) — two different categories of taxation on non-Muslims

concepts.name: Firuz Shah Tughluq's Administrative Reforms: Welfare vs. Decentralization Trade-off
key_dimensions: Positive reforms: hospitals (Dar-ul-Shafa), canals (largest irrigation network of Sultanate), employment bureau (Diwan-i-Khairat)
Negative consequences: hereditary offices/iqtas weakened central authority; slave corps (1,80,000 slaves) became a financial burden
Abolition of torture and mutilation as punishment — humanitarian but seen as weakening deterrence
UPSC trap: Firuz is often portrayed as a 'benevolent' ruler — question may ask about structural weaknesses his policies created

concepts.name: Diwan-i-Bandagan: Department of Slaves under Firuz Shah Tughluq
key_dimensions: Unique institution: dedicated department to manage the Sultan's enormous slave corps (~1,80,000 slaves)
Slaves used as administrators, soldiers, and artisans — not merely domestic servants
Financial strain: maintenance of slaves cited as a major reason for Sultanate's fiscal stress post-Firuz
Comparison with early Slave Dynasty (Ilbari Turks) where slaves held power informally vs. Firuz's formal institutionalization

concepts.name: Village-Level Administration: Khut, Muqaddam, and Patwari
key_dimensions: Khut (superior landholder/zamindar) and Muqaddam (village headman) as intermediaries between state and peasantry
Alauddin Khalji's attempt to eliminate Khut/Muqaddam privileges (exemptions, personal perquisites) — and why this was revolutionary
Patwari: village accountant maintaining land records — continuity from Sultanate through Mughal period
UPSC trap: Alauddin's revenue reforms targeted these intermediary classes specifically — not a general agrarian reform

concepts.name: Central Judicial Structure: Hierarchy from Sultan to Village Qazi
key_dimensions: Sultan as the ultimate court of appeal (Mazalim court) — dispensing justice beyond Shariat limitations
Qazi-ul-Quzat → Provincial Qazi → District Qazi → Village Qazi: four-tier hierarchy
Parallel Hindu customary law (through Panchayats) operating alongside Islamic Shariat courts — dual legal system
UPSC trap: Mazalim courts (Sultan's personal justice) operated OUTSIDE Shariat — this is a key distinction from the Qazi system

concepts.name: Nobles' Classification: Distinction between Amiran-i-Sadah and Khans/Maliks
key_dimensions: Hierarchy of titles: Sultan → Khan → Malik → Amir — specific ranks with corresponding revenue and military obligations
Amiran-i-Hazara (commanders of 1000) vs. Amiran-i-Sadah (commanders of 100) — UPSC may test decimal military-administrative units
Ethnic composition shift: from exclusively Turkish nobles (early period) to inclusion of Afghans, Indians, converted Hindus (later period)
UPSC trap: the term 'Forty' (Chalisa/Turkan-i-Chahalgani) refers specifically to Iltutmish's council of forty Turkish nobles — NOT a generic term for all Sultanate nobility

concepts.name: Barid System: Intelligence and Postal Network
key_dimensions: Barid-i-Mumalik: head of the intelligence/postal department reporting directly to Sultan
Dual function: carrying state correspondence (postal) AND gathering intelligence on governors/nobles
Alauddin Khalji's expansion of the Barid system as part of his spy network alongside Munhiyan (secret agents)
UPSC trap: Barid is NOT merely a postal system — its intelligence function was primary in the Sultanate context

concepts.name: Muhammad bin Tughluq's Administrative Experiments: Rationale and Failure Analysis
key_dimensions: Transfer of capital to Daulatabad: strategic rationale (central location, defense against Mongols) vs. actual failure reasons
Token currency experiment: structural flaw (state could not prevent forgery; no guarantee mechanism) — NOT simply 'ahead of its time'
Taxation in Doab: timing with famine made a possibly rational policy catastrophic — UPSC trap on separating policy intent from outcome
Khurasan and Qarachil expeditions as evidence of imperial overreach — administrative capacity vs. territorial ambition mismatch

concepts.name: Diwan-i-Mustakhraj: Department for Recovery of Revenue Arrears
key_dimensions: Established by Alauddin Khalji specifically to recover outstanding revenue dues from Muqtis and local chiefs
Significance: indicates that regular Diwan-i-Wizarat was insufficient for enforcement — a supplementary coercive mechanism
UPSC trap: this is a SEPARATE department from Diwan-i-Wizarat, not a subdivision — often confused
Reflects Alauddin's broader strategy of bypassing entrenched intermediaries through direct state intervention

concepts.name: Sultanate's Relationship with the Ulema: Theocracy vs. Sultanate Sovereignty
key_dimensions: UPSC trap: Delhi Sultanate was NOT a theocracy — Sultans regularly overrode Ulema advice (Alauddin explicitly stated he made policy without consulting Shariat)
Ulema's administrative roles: Qazis, Sadrs, teachers in madrasas — embedded in state structure but not controlling it
Firuz Shah Tughluq as the exception: more deferential to Ulema than predecessors — specific policy examples (persecution of Mahdi movement)
Barani's political theory (Fatawa-i-Jahandari) advocating Turkish aristocratic rule — NOT pure Islamic governance — a nuanced UPSC angle
